item.title: investingLive Americas FX news wrap 30 Oct: It’s a wrap: Nasdaq tumbles as AI costs worry investors; Fed speakers keep hikes in play
item.description:
• Nasdaq suffers worst month since March 2025 as technology stocks tumble
  • Bitcoin tests key support as Binance security fears weigh
  • Week ahead: Elections, rate decisions and jobs take center stage
  • Earnings next week: Can Apple, Palantir and AMD restore confidence?
  • Fed’s Logan: At least two more quarter-point rate hikes needed
  • Carney: Canada, EU working toward deepest possible partnership, short of accession
  • Fed’s Daly: AI matters for near- and medium-term policy
  • Fitch on UK Budget: Policy continuity leaves a tough delivery challenge
  • Fed's Barkin: Direction of travel is straightforward for the Fed
  • Canada GDP for August 0.0% vs 0.2% estimate
  • US employment cost index for Q3 +0.8% vs +0.8% expected
  • Morning Kickstart: Tech hammered as Amazon and Intel tumble; oil rises despite peace talk
  • investingLive European session wrap: AI spending fears spook tech stocks; dollar falls alongside yields, gold

October ended with investors taking a harder look at the cost of the AI boom. Technology led a broad stock-market decline as disappointing reactions to Amazon and Intel earnings reinforced concerns about spending, profitability and cash flow. Strong demand remains part of the story, but investors are becoming more demanding about when that demand translates into returns.

The cross-market moves were revealing. Treasury yields declined even as several Fed officials argued for further tightening. Oil moved higher, keeping inflation concerns alive, while gold failed to benefit from lower yields. Bonds attracted defensive demand, but the protection did not extend across every traditional haven.

Dollar finishes mixed after recovering earlier losses

The dollar was mixed in the supplied late-session snapshot. Its strongest performance was against the euro, with EURUSD down 0.13% at 1.1164. Its weakest performance was against sterling, with GBPUSD up 0.11% at 1.3390.

USDJPY slipped 0.06% to 157.59, while USDCHF rose 0.05% to 0.8246. USDCAD edged down 0.06% to 1.3979 despite disappointing Canadian growth data. AUDUSD gained 0.07% to 0.7032, while NZDUSD fell 0.07% to 0.5629.

The mixed finish marked a recovery from the dollar’s broader weakness earlier in the session. Falling U.S. yields provided a headwind, but the currency market did not deliver a uniform risk-off response.

Treasury yields fall despite calls for more tightening

Treasury yields were lower across the curve in the supplied snapshot. The 2-year yield fell 6.43 basis points to 4.5917%, the 5-year declined 7.87 basis points to 4.7233%, the 10-year dropped 5.86 basis points to 4.9303%, and the 30-year eased 1.76 basis points to 5.3114%.

The larger declines in shorter and intermediate maturities steepened the curve. The move was consistent with defensive demand as stocks weakened, even though the Fed commentary offered little reassurance that the tightening cycle was finished. Lower yields alone were insufficient to offset the concerns facing technology shares.

U.S. stocks: Nasdaq leads the retreat

The supplied end-of-day index readings showed:

  • Dow industrial average: −573.08 points, or −1.09%, at 51,775.17.

  • S&P 500: −140.32 points, or −1.82%, at 7,580.07.

  • Nasdaq Composite: −747.73 points, or −2.86%, at 25,437.00.

  • Russell 2000: −47.37 points, or −1.66%, at 2,811.84.

  • Nasdaq 100: −1,017.66 points, or −3.46%, at 28,384.85.

The selling extended beyond technology, but the Nasdaq indices carried the heaviest burden. The Dow held up better on a relative basis, although a decline of more than 570 points still reflected a difficult session.

AI faces questions about financing and returns

Amazon and Intel remained central to the earnings concerns. Investors questioned how much spending would be required to sustain AI growth and how quickly that investment would produce stronger profits and cash flow.

A separate Financial Times report covered by InvestingLive added a financing concern: Blackstone reportedly told Anthropic that it might not obtain an investment-grade credit rating after its IPO. This was a reported possibility, rather than a ratings decision, but it sharpened the focus on borrowing costs. Intel was down more than 30% in that afternoon report, with substantial losses across chip and infrastructure suppliers including AMD, Arm, Marvell, Astera Labs and Coherent. Those were intraday readings.

European stocks mostly lower

European markets also finished mostly lower, with the UK holding a modest gain:

  • Germany’s DAX: −221.47 points, or −0.85%, at 25,818.22.

  • France’s CAC 40: −0.58 points, or −0.01%, at 7,969.43.

  • UK’s FTSE 100: +7.73 points, or +0.07%, at 10,729.79.

  • Spain’s IBEX: −204.70 points, or −1.09%, at 18,652.90.

  • Italy’s FTSE MIB: −501.39 points, or −1.02%, at 49,290.91.

Fed speak: More tightening remains on the table

Today’s Fed commentary carried a predominantly hawkish message, although the speakers differed in how directly they addressed the next policy move. Barkin favored gradual adjustment, Musalem argued for another increase soon, and Logan outlined a minimum of two additional quarter-point hikes. Daly concentrated on AI’s implications for the Fed’s inflation and employment objectives.

Richmond Fed President Barkin described the direction of policy as straightforward, with the pace still open to debate. He favored a gradual approach but pointed to resilient consumer spending, broad business cost pressures and companies preparing to pass those costs to customers. His comments on AI were particularly relevant to the day’s market debate: the investment surge is adding demand and straining supply chains, creating inflation pressures that monetary policy can lean against. His assessment suggested that economic resilience continues to give the Fed room to address persistent inflation.

San Francisco Fed President Daly focused on how AI affects both price stability and employment. She emphasized that those effects matter for policy in the near and medium term. Her remarks did not establish a preference for a hike or a pause. The takeaway was that AI’s effects on the economy are already relevant to current monetary policy decisions.

St. Louis Fed President Musalem delivered a more explicit call for action, saying rates would need to rise again soon. He viewed monetary policy and overall financial conditions as accommodative, with inflation unlikely to ease sufficiently without additional Fed action. Higher bond yields had tightened conditions, but not enough in his assessment. His preference was to act earlier in smaller increments, reducing the risk that delayed action eventually requires a sharper adjustment. A strong economy and labor market supported that approach, while inflation risks remained tilted higher.

Dallas Fed President Logan was the most specific about the amount of tightening she considered necessary. She called for at least two more quarter-point increases to make policy modestly restrictive, followed by a pause to assess whether further action was needed. Skipping a meeting, in her view, would not change the destination. Gradual adjustments could help households, businesses and investors adapt, but she regarded the lack of progress toward the 2% inflation target as unacceptable. Her message made clear that a pause should not automatically be interpreted as the end of tightening.

For traders, the distinction matters: Treasury yields fell on the day, but these remarks did not amount to a dovish shift from the Fed.

Economic data: Labor costs moderate, growth signals soften

The U.S. Employment Cost Index rose 0.8% in the third quarter, matching expectations and slowing from 0.9%. Wage growth eased to 0.7% from 0.9%, while benefit costs increased 0.9%, down from 1.0%. The report offered some reassurance on compensation pressures, although it did not resolve the broader inflation concerns raised by Fed officials.

Chicago PMI fell to 55.3, below the 56.1 estimate and down from 58.8. Activity remained above the 50 dividing line, but the pace of expansion slowed.

Canada’s August GDP was unchanged versus expectations for 0.2% growth. The advance estimate pointed to a 0.1% decline in September, reinforcing the picture of an economy struggling to build momentum.

German preliminary inflation also came in softer than expected. Annual CPI and harmonized inflation both slowed to 2.8%, below forecasts of 3.0% and 3.1%, respectively.

Oil rises as Middle East risks persist

WTI crude traded at $102.89, up $0.89 or 0.87% in the supplied snapshot.

InvestingLive’s oil coverage highlighted Houthi attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure and reports of U.S. preparations for potential strikes on Iran. Those developments kept supply risks in focus heading into the weekend. Elevated energy prices also complicated the inflation outlook, even as Treasury yields declined.

Gold and silver join the selling

Spot gold fell approximately $146.24, or 3.64%, to $3,874.33. Silver dropped $3.0644, or 5.88%, to $49.0756. Copper also declined 1.75% to $6.4870.

Gold’s weakness stood out because Treasury yields were lower. That would normally provide support, but sellers retained control. InvestingLive’s gold analysis identified liquidation pressure associated with equity losses as a possible explanation: investors needing cash can sell liquid holdings such as gold to meet obligations elsewhere. That remains an interpretation of the selling, rather than a confirmed explanation for every transaction.

Silver’s larger percentage decline, alongside weaker copper, also left the more industrially sensitive metals under pressure.

Bitcoin remains under pressure

Bitcoin traded at $76,803, down $989 or 1.27% in the supplied snapshot.

The broader retreat from risk assets was compounded by concerns surrounding the reported Binance security breach. InvestingLive’s crypto coverage described exchange-security anxiety and leveraged liquidations as additional sources of pressure. Falling Treasury yields offered little relief as investors weighed both market-wide weakness and crypto-specific uncertainty.

Next week: U.S. elections, jobs and central-bank decisions

The November 2–6 calendar brings several important tests for markets, led by Tuesday’s U.S. midterm elections and Friday’s employment report. The results will help shape expectations for government policy, economic growth and the Fed’s next move.

Monday starts with the U.S. ISM manufacturing report at 10:00 AM ET. Wednesday brings ADP employment at 8:15 AM ET and ISM services at 10:00 AM ET. Beyond the headline readings, traders will watch the employment and prices components for evidence of whether activity is slowing while inflation pressures persist.

Tuesday’s midterm elections will determine control of the House and Senate, with implications for taxes, spending, regulation and the administration’s legislative agenda. The September JOLTS report, due at 10:00 AM ET, provides another measure of labor demand ahead of payrolls.

Central banks also remain in focus. The Reserve Bank of Australia announces its decision Tuesday, November 3, Australian time—Monday evening in the U.S.—with several major banks expecting a 25-basis-point hike to 4.85%. The Bank of England follows Thursday with its rate decision and updated economic forecasts. Both events will test how policymakers balance inflation risks against the effects of tighter policy.

Thursday brings U.S. jobless claims and preliminary third-quarter productivity and labor costs at 8:30 AM ET. Friday is the main economic event: U.S. payrolls, unemployment and average hourly earnings at 8:30 AM ET, alongside Canada’s employment report. Preliminary University of Michigan consumer sentiment follows at 10:00 AM ET, with inflation expectations another important barometer. Together, the reports will help determine whether the economy remains resilient enough to support further Fed tightening.

What traders carry forward

The next session begins with three connected questions: can technology shares stabilize, can Middle East risks ease enough to take pressure off oil, and will incoming data justify the additional tightening several Fed officials favor? Friday showed that lower Treasury yields alone are not enough to restore confidence when earnings, financing costs and inflation remain in question.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Nasdaq suffers worst month since March 2025 as technology stocks tumble
item.description:
US stocks are trading sharply lower in the final session of October, with the Nasdaq indices again leading the declines. The selling caps a difficult month for technology, with the Nasdaq Composite down 5.30%—its worst monthly performance since March 2025.

However, the monthly performance shows a market that has been far from uniform. The Dow and Russell 2000 remain positive, highlighting the gap between battered technology stocks and pockets of strength elsewhere.

Today’s market: Nasdaq leads the selling

At the latest snapshot:

  • Dow: Down 573.08 points, or 1.09%, at 51,775.17.

  • S&P 500: Down 140.32 points, or 1.82%, at 7,580.07.

  • Nasdaq Composite: Down 747.73 points, or 2.86%, at 25,437.00.

  • Russell 2000: Down 47.37 points, or 1.66%, at 2,811.84.

  • Nasdaq 100: Down 1,017.66 points, or 3.46%, at 28,384.85.

October performance: Dow outpaces Nasdaq 100 by 8.35 percentage points

For the month:

  • Dow: Up 1.70%.

  • S&P 500: Down 0.93%.

  • Nasdaq Composite: Down 5.30%.

  • Russell 2000: Up 0.53%.

  • Nasdaq 100: Down 6.65%.

The Dow’s 8.35-percentage-point advantage over the Nasdaq 100 underscores the extent of the divergence. Investors have continued to reward selected companies while aggressively reducing exposure to others.

The breadth of that list matters. Selling has extended across chipmakers, equipment suppliers, connectivity companies and AI infrastructure names. Buyers have struggled to find protection across much of the investment theme.

Those gains help explain why the broader market has held up better than the Nasdaq indices. There have been opportunities outside the hardest-hit technology names.

Market breadth: Sellers have the upper hand today

Today’s participation shows considerable pressure beneath the surface:

  • Nasdaq: 778 advancing versus 2,455 declining—roughly three decliners for every advancer.

The S&P 500’s more balanced breadth contrasts with the heavier selling across Nasdaq-listed stocks. Nevertheless, declining stocks outnumber advancing stocks across all four measures.

What comes next: Can technology buyers regain control?

For buyers, the challenge is to show that technology can stabilize. A rebound in a few large names would help, but broader participation would provide a more convincing signal that selling pressure is easing.

For sellers, the next question is whether weakness spreads further into the areas that have supported the broader market. The Dow and Russell 2000 remain positive for October, but today’s declines show that those areas are also feeling pressure.

Next week’s earnings: Another test for technology

The November 2–6 earnings calendar brings another important test for sentiment following October’s technology selloff. Eight reports to watch:

  • Monday, November 2: Apple and Palantir—both after the close.

  • Tuesday, November 3: AMD and Arista Networks—both after the close.

  • Wednesday, November 4: Uber before the open; Qualcomm, Arm and AppLovin after the close.

For the technology reports, the focus will be whether growth, margins and guidance can give buyers a reason to step back in. AI demand remains central, but investors will also want evidence that spending is translating into stronger profits and cash flow.

item.title: Bitcoin tests key support as Binance security fears weigh
item.description:
Bitcoin is trading to new session lows, bringing its 100-day moving average at $76,139 into focus. The low so far has reached $76,172, leaving the price just $33 above a key technical level that could help define the next move.

Sentiment has been unsettled by reports of an alleged Binance security breach. The account circulating describes $6.3B of assets being drained from wallets across multiple blockchains over a 20 minute period on Thursday, raising concerns about customer funds, exchange security and potential spillover across the cryptocurrency ecosystem. North Korea is being targeted for the breach.  

Security scares can put additional pressure on prices when leveraged positions are involved. Falling prices trigger margin calls and forced liquidations, which can generate further selling. That process can magnify the initial reaction as traders reduce exposure and wait for clarity.

The broader backdrop also remains challenging, with inflation risks, growth concerns and geopolitical tensions weighing on risk appetite.

The 100-day MA becomes the immediate barometer

Technically, for Bitcoin traders, the immediate question is whether buyers can defend the 100-day moving average at $76,139.

The proximity of the session low gives buyers a clearly defined level to lean against, with close risk if support fails. Holding above the moving average would provide an opportunity for a corrective bounce, although buyers would still need follow-through to show that selling pressure is easing.

Conversely, a sustained break below $76,139 would weaken that defense and give sellers another technical reason to press lower.The low from September at $74,925 would be the next target followed by the 200 day MA at $73,112 and the 50% midpoint of the move up from the end of June low at $72,554.  

The news is creating uncertainty. The technicals provide a level against which traders can define their bias and manage their risk. Stay above and the buyers remain in play. Move below and the sellers keep the control. 

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Week ahead: Elections, rate decisions and jobs take center stage
item.description:
Next week’s calendar gives traders plenty to work with. US congressional elections bring political uncertainty, the Reserve Bank of Australia and Bank of England are expected to raise rates, and Friday delivers employment reports from both the US and Canada.

The central question is whether growth, inflation and employment support a more restrictive policy outlook. For traders, the releases will provide the catalysts. The technical levels will help define the bias, risk and targets as those headlines hit.

Monday, November 2: US manufacturing and the RBA decision

The week starts with US manufacturing before attention shifts to Australia late in the North American evening.

  • 10:00 AM ET – US ISM Manufacturing PMI – Forecast: 54.7 – Previous: 54.5.

  • 10:30 PM ET – RBA cash rate decision – Forecast: 4.85% – Previous: 4.60%.

  • 10:30 PM ET – RBA Monetary Policy Statement and Rate Statement.

  • 11:30 PM ET – RBA press conference.

The manufacturing index is expected to edge higher, remaining above the 50 level that separates expansion from contraction. Traders will also watch prices paid, new orders and employment for clues about inflation pressure and the durability of growth.

For the AUDUSD, the calendar points to a 25-basis-point RBA hike. The reaction will depend on the guidance as well as the decision. Does the central bank leave the door open to additional tightening, or suggest policy is approaching a sufficient level?

Tuesday, November 3: US elections, job openings and New Zealand employment

US congressional elections dominate the political calendar, while JOLTS provides another reading on labor demand.

  • 2:30 AM ET – Swiss CPI, monthly – Forecast: 0.0% – Previous: 0.0%.

  • 10:00 AM ET – US JOLTS job openings – Forecast: 7.11 million – Previous: 7.08 million.

  • All day – US congressional elections.

  • 11:00 AM ET – Bank of Canada Governor Macklem speaks.

  • 4:45 PM ET – New Zealand employment change, quarterly – Forecast: 0.4% – Previous: 0.5%.

  • 4:45 PM ET – New Zealand unemployment rate – Forecast: 5.5% – Previous: 5.6%.

US elections: Control of Congress is the key prize

Tuesday’s elections will determine control of the House and Senate—and how much room President Trump has to advance his legislative agenda during the second half of his term.

Senate: Key contests to watch include Georgia, North Carolina, Maine and Michigan. Georgia’s seat held by Democrat Jon Ossoff and Maine’s seat held by Republican Susan Collins are central battlegrounds. Open-seat contests in North Carolina and Michigan also give both parties important opportunities. New Hampshire’s open seat is another race worth watching.

House: Control could come down to a relatively small number of competitive districts, particularly in California, New York, Pennsylvania, Michigan and Arizona. Suburban voters and districts with closely divided presidential results will be especially important.

For markets: Republican control of both chambers would give the administration more room to pursue tax, spending and regulatory legislation. Democratic control of either chamber would create divided government, increasing the need for negotiation over budgets and major legislation. Investors will watch the implications for Treasury borrowing, energy, healthcare and corporate taxes.

What would it take to flip control of Congress?

Democrats need a net gain of three House seats and four Senate seats to take control of both chambers.

In the House, Republicans emerged with a 220–215 majority. A net Democratic gain of three seats would shift that balance to 218–217, giving Democrats a narrow majority.

In the Senate, Republicans held a 53–47 advantage. Democrats need a net gain of four seats to secure a 51–49 majority. Gaining only three would leave the chamber split 50–50, with Vice President JD Vance’s tie-breaking vote keeping Republicans in control.

The key word is net: each seat a party loses must be offset by another pickup. For markets, a Democratic takeover of either chamber would bring divided government, making major tax and spending legislation more dependent on negotiations.

New Zealand’s report is expected to show slightly slower employment growth alongside a lower unemployment rate. Wages and participation will help explain whether that combination reflects a firmer labor market.

Wednesday, November 4: Eurozone inflation and US services

Inflation in Europe and activity in the larger US services sector move into focus.

  • 5:00 AM ET – Eurozone core CPI flash estimate, annual – Forecast: 2.5% – Previous: 2.5%.

  • 5:00 AM ET – Eurozone headline CPI flash estimate, annual – Forecast: 4.0% – Previous: 3.8%.

  • 10:00 AM ET – US ISM Services PMI – Forecast: 54.9 – Previous: 54.9.

The expected rise in headline eurozone inflation would complicate the policy picture, even with core inflation holding steady.

In the US, an unchanged services reading would signal continued expansion. The details matter: stronger prices paid alongside softer employment could produce a very different market reaction than broad strength across new orders, business activity and hiring.

Thursday, November 5: BOE decision and Canada’s budget

The Bank of England headlines a busy session that also includes US claims, several central bank speakers and Canada’s annual budget.

  • 7:00 AM ET – BOE bank rate decision – Forecast: 4.00% – Previous: 3.75%.

  • 7:00 AM ET – BOE MPC vote split, hike–hold–cut – Forecast: 7–0–2 – Previous: 3–0–6.

  • 7:00 AM ET – BOE Monetary Policy Report and Policy Summary.

  • 7:30 AM ET – BOE Governor Bailey speaks.

  • 7:40 AM ET – SNB Chairman Schlegel speaks.

  • 8:30 AM ET – US initial unemployment claims – Forecast: 197,000 – Previous: 194,000.

  • 10:30 AM ET – Bank of Canada Governor Macklem speaks.

  • 1:00 PM ET – ECB President Lagarde speaks.

  • 4:00 PM ET – Canada annual budget release.

The supplied calendar points to a 25-basis-point BOE hike, with a sharp change in the expected voting balance. Sterling traders will watch whether the inflation forecasts and Bailey’s comments reinforce the need for further tightening.

Canada’s budget adds a fiscal catalyst for the CAD, with spending, borrowing and growth assumptions likely to attract attention ahead of Friday’s employment report.

Friday, November 6: US and Canadian jobs headline the week

Friday brings the week’s biggest scheduled data test, with both employment reports arriving at 8:30 AM ET.

  • 8:30 AM ET – US nonfarm payrolls – Forecast: +63,000 – Previous: +29,000.

  • 8:30 AM ET – US unemployment rate – Forecast: 4.2% – Previous: 4.2%.

  • 8:30 AM ET – US average hourly earnings, monthly – Forecast: 0.3% – Previous: 0.1%.

  • 8:30 AM ET – Canada employment change – Forecast: +14,500 – Previous: −68,300.

  • 8:30 AM ET – Canada unemployment rate – Forecast: 6.5% – Previous: 6.5%.

  • 10:00 AM ET – Canada Ivey PMI – Forecast: 57.7 – Previous: 58.2.

  • 10:00 AM ET – Preliminary University of Michigan consumer sentiment – Forecast: 47.8 – Previous: 48.0.

  • 10:00 AM ET – Preliminary University of Michigan inflation expectations – Forecast: Not listed – Previous: 4.7%.

  • 11:00 AM ET – BOJ Governor Ueda speaks.

  • All day – New Zealand parliamentary elections, as listed on the supplied calendar.

US payroll growth is expected to improve but remain modest, while wage growth is forecast to accelerate. Soft hiring alongside firmer wages would leave traders weighing slower growth against persistent inflation pressure. Payroll revisions will also matter.

Canada is expected to recover only part of the previous employment decline. With both reports released simultaneously, the USDCAD could see a sharp initial reaction as traders compare the relative strength of the two economies.

The trading focus: Let the reaction confirm the story

There are several opportunities for expectations to shift during the week. A rate hike can support a currency, but the follow-through will depend on what comes next. Stronger employment can lift yields, while the wage details may change how investors interpret the same report.

Watch the first move, then watch whether the price can hold its break. A sustained break shifts the bias. A failed break puts the other side back in play. With elections, central banks and jobs competing for attention, clearly defined risk will be especially valuable.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Earnings next week: Can Apple, Palantir and AMD restore confidence?
item.description:
This week was not so great for investors looking to earnings to support the stock market. Some big-name reports brought sharp selling, highlighting how quickly buyers can turn into sellers when results or expectations disappoint.

Intel was a clear example. Adjusted earnings of $0.52 per share beat the $0.41 estimate, but revenue of $16.50 billion fell short of the $16.60 billion forecast. The earnings beat offered little protection: shares were down approximately 25.7% in Friday morning trading.

Amazon also came under pressure, falling approximately 6.3% in Thursday’s after-hours trading before  bouncing back. Its report kept attention on the balance between growth, investment spending and the cash flow left for shareholders.

Those reactions raise the stakes for next week. Beating the headline earnings estimate may get investors’ attention, but the outlook, margins and spending plans will determine whether that attention translates into buying.

Apple and Palantir headline Monday’s after-close reports, followed by AMD, Super Micro Computer and Arista Networks on Tuesday. Uber, Qualcomm, Arm and AppLovin add to the technology focus on Wednesday.

The central question for the AI trade remains: Is demand strong enough to justify the spending—and translate into stronger earnings and cash flow?

Monday: Apple and Palantir set the tone

Before the open: Check Point Software, Estée Lauder, Marriott International and Tower Semiconductor.

After the close: Apple, Palantir and Roku.

Apple will put iPhone demand, services growth, China performance and the holiday-quarter outlook in focus. Investors will also look for evidence that AI features are providing a compelling reason for customers to upgrade their devices.

Palantir faces a different test: whether commercial and government demand can support continued rapid growth while maintaining profitability. The forward guidance will be particularly important in determining whether the results give buyers enough reason to step in.

Roku will offer another perspective on advertising demand and consumers’ streaming habits.

Tuesday: AI infrastructure faces a major test

Before the open: Shopify, Pfizer, Marathon Petroleum, Eaton and Apollo Global Management.

After the close: AMD, Super Micro Computer, Arista Networks, Astera Labs, Booking Holdings and Amgen.

Tuesday brings a broad examination of the AI infrastructure supply chain. AMD’s data-center performance and AI accelerator outlook will be key barometers for chip demand.

For Super Micro Computer, investors will look beyond server sales to margins, working-capital needs and cash generation. Strong demand is helpful, but shareholders also want to see that delivering those systems produces attractive returns.

Arista Networks and Astera Labs will provide insight into networking and connectivity spending. Eaton adds another piece of the puzzle through electrical equipment and the power requirements of expanding data centers.

Outside the AI trade, Shopify will offer a read on merchant activity and online spending, while Booking Holdings will provide an update on travel demand.

Wednesday: Chips, software and consumers in focus

Before the open: Uber, Novo Nordisk, Datadog, GlobalFoundries, McDonald’s and CVS Health.

After the close: AppLovin, Qualcomm, Arm, Coherent, Cava and Dutch Bros.

Uber’s bookings, profitability and guidance will offer a window into mobility and delivery demand. McDonald’s, Cava and Dutch Bros will help show where consumers are spending—and how much promotions, pricing and operating costs are affecting margins.

Qualcomm and Arm will shift attention toward smartphone demand, licensing trends and opportunities beyond handsets. Coherent will add another update on optical communications demand.

Datadog’s results will offer insight into cloud activity and enterprise spending. AppLovin’s advertising growth, profitability and outlook will be another important barometer for technology sentiment.

Novo Nordisk will put weight-loss and diabetes treatments in focus, including sales growth, competition and pricing. CVS Health will add a perspective on healthcare costs and operating performance.

Thursday: Optical demand, cloud spending and travel

Before the open: Unity, Cardinal Health, Celsius, Core Scientific and Cigna.

After the close: Lumentum, Applied Optoelectronics, Cloudflare and Airbnb.

Lumentum and Applied Optoelectronics will extend the examination of optical connectivity and data-center investment. Investors will watch whether demand is translating into stronger sales, improving margins and a constructive outlook.

Cloudflare will provide another check on enterprise technology spending and the ability to convert customer demand into profitable growth.

Airbnb’s bookings and guidance will offer a further read on travel demand, while Cigna’s report will keep healthcare utilization and medical costs in focus.

Friday: Healthcare and consumer spending close the week

Before the open: Moderna, Humana and Under Armour.

Humana’s medical-cost trends and guidance will be closely watched for signs of pressure on profitability. Moderna’s update will focus attention on its commercial outlook, expenses and development pipeline.

Under Armour will provide another perspective on discretionary spending, promotional activity and margins. Investors will look for evidence that efforts to improve the business are gaining traction.

The key question: Will the results bring buyers back?

This week showed that an earnings beat alone does not guarantee a higher stock price. Investors want confidence in what comes next: sustainable demand, controlled costs, stronger cash generation and guidance that supports expectations.

Next week’s reports will help determine whether the recent selling attracts buyers or whether disappointing outlooks give sellers another reason to press.

For traders, the price reaction remains the barometer. Can a stock rally on good news and hold its gains? Can it absorb disappointing news and defend support? A failed rally at resistance keeps sellers in control. A recovery above broken technical levels gives buyers something to build on.

In her view, higher long-term yields have not created enough of a drag to remove the need for further policy action. item.title: Fitch on UK Budget: Policy continuity leaves a tough delivery challenge
item.description:
Fitch’s assessment of the UK Budget points to a familiar problem: setting out a path to stronger public finances is one thing. Delivering it is another.

The ratings agency sees broad continuity in government policy, but warns that the plans still leave a sizeable delivery challenge. It continues to anticipate significant slippage against spending plans and says fiscal consolidation becomes much more challenging to deliver from 2027.

That puts the emphasis on execution. The key barometer will be whether actual spending and borrowing follow the government’s projected path.

Spending discipline remains the central concern

Fitch’s warning about spending slippage suggests it expects the government to struggle to keep expenditure within its planned limits.

If spending exceeds those assumptions, the government would need to offset the difference through higher revenues, savings elsewhere or additional borrowing. Each carries consequences for the economic outlook and the credibility of the fiscal plan.

For investors, the question is whether the projected improvement in public finances can survive the pressures that emerge along the way.

Election politics add another layer of risk

Fitch also sees moderately greater policy risk closer to the next general election.

The implication is that the political willingness to deliver difficult fiscal measures could weaken as an election approaches. Pressure to support households, protect public services or offer new commitments could complicate the planned adjustment.

That matters because Fitch already sees the consolidation becoming harder from 2027. The economic and political challenges could increasingly overlap.

Investment measures do not materially change the picture

Fitch notes that support through the National Wealth Fund and British Business Bank will increase. However, it does not see the Burnham government as meaningfully lifting its infrastructure spending plans.

It also expects measures allowing mayors to spend a portion of income tax revenues from 2028 to be broadly fiscally neutral initially.

Those initiatives therefore do little to change Fitch’s central concern: the difficulty of delivering the overall fiscal path.

The market takeaway

My reading is that this is a warning about delivery and credibility. Broad policy continuity provides a framework, but the spending numbers still have to hold.

For gilt and sterling traders, these headlines identify a risk to monitor rather than establish a market direction on their own. If confidence in the fiscal path deteriorates, upward pressure on borrowing costs could become a concern. Sterling’s response would depend on whether higher yields reflect stronger economic expectations or greater fiscal risk.

The budget sets the targets. The spending and borrowing data will show whether the government can deliver.

As a review, the UK Budget was delivered on Wednesday, October 28. Its main aim was to provide targeted cost-of-living relief while preserving plans to reduce borrowing, with difficult spending decisions still ahead.

  • Household support: A £100 energy payment for eligible households in England’s council tax bands A–D, with funding for comparable support elsewhere in the UK. The electricity VAT cut and temporary 5p fuel-duty reduction are extended until July 2027.
  • Targeted tax increases: The bank corporation tax surcharge rises temporarily from 3% to 6%. From April 2027, tax rates on savings and property income will be 24%, 44% and 49%.
  • Wages and businesses: The National Living Wage rises 3.9% to £13.21 an hour in April 2027. Retail, hospitality and leisure businesses receive expanded business-rate relief.
  • Housing: An additional £1.5 billion supports social and affordable housing, alongside a new equity-loan scheme for first-time buyers and a First Time Buyer ISA from April 2029.
  • Weaker growth, higher inflation: The OBR cut its 2027 growth forecast to 1.0% from 1.6%, while raising its inflation forecast to 3.4% from 2.0%. It judged that the budget measures make little difference to those forecasts.
  • Limited fiscal room: The government meets its fiscal rules on the forecasts, but the buffer against its day-to-day budget target is only £15 billion in 2029/30. Borrowing is projected to average approximately £13 billion a year more than previously forecast over 2026/27–2030/31.

THE GBPUSD has moved higher this week after bottoming on Wednesday

Technically, the GBPUSD bottomed on Wednesday near the swing level at 1.32729, giving buyers a technical floor to lean against. The subsequent recovery initially attracted sellers near the falling 100-hour moving average, but buyers broke through that resistance during yesterday’s trade and extended above the 200-hour moving average.

Those breaks shifted the near-term bias toward the buyers. The 100-hour moving average at 1.3338 and the 200-hour moving average at 1.33585 became support levels to watch on a correction.

Buyers reach the 200-day moving average

The rally gathered momentum today, with the price breaking above two additional hurdles:

  • 100-day moving average: 1.33857

  • 50% midpoint of the decline from the August high: 1.34056

Those breaks opened the door for a test of the 200-day moving average at 1.34277. The session high reached 1.3433, taking the price modestly above that longer-term barometer.

However, buyers could not sustain the break. Sellers leaned against the area, and the price rotated lower during the North American session.

That makes the 200-day moving average an important ceiling. Buyers reached a major target, but they still need to establish acceptance above it to strengthen the bullish case.

The pullback puts buyers to the test

The rotation lower has taken the price back below the 50% midpoint at 1.34056 and the 100-day moving average at 1.33857. Giving back those breaks takes some of the momentum out of the rally and gives sellers an opportunity to regain control.

The 1.33857 level becomes the immediate barometer. Staying below it would keep sellers in play and leave the 200-hour moving average at 1.33585 as the next downside target. Below that, the 100-hour moving average at 1.3338 would come into focus.

Conversely, a move back above 1.33857, followed by 1.34056, would help buyers steady the technical picture and put the 1.34277–1.3433 resistance area back in their sights.

The recovery from Wednesday’s low has cleared several important hurdles. The question now is how much of that technical progress buyers can defend.

item.title: Gold tumbles despite lower yields. Technicals show the way.
item.description:
Lower yields fail to provide support

Gold is moving sharply lower despite a decline in US Treasury yields. The 10-year yield is down 5 basis points to 4.939%, a move that would normally provide some support for the precious metal. Instead, gold is trading near $3900, down roughly $120, or 3%, after reaching a session low near $3891.

That divergence is telling. Buyers have a potentially supportive move in the bond market, but they are struggling to turn it into buying momentum. When the price cannot rally on a favorable development, traders need to respect what the price action is saying.

Connecting the dots from a fundamental or interest-rate perspective may be difficult. The technicals, however, are providing a clearer roadmap.

Moving averages put sellers in control

On the hourly chart, gold moved back below its 100- and 200-hour moving averages on October 19. The downside did not accelerate immediately, but those moving averages helped form a ceiling, keeping the bearish bias intact. By October 22, downside momentum began to build.

The subsequent decline took the price to $3959.37 before buyers managed a recovery. However, that rebound stalled on Wednesday near $4080, against the 200-hour moving average.

That failed recovery was an important clue. Buyers had an opportunity to challenge the bearish bias, but they could not push through a key technical barometer. Sellers could lean against the moving average with defined risk—and the subsequent rotation lower rewarded that decision.

A broken floor accelerates the decline

The next leg lower has continued into today with little sustained upside correction. Once the price broke below the $3942.71–$3959.37 swing area, selling accelerated, taking gold toward $3891.

That break matters because an established support area gives traders a reference point. Above it, buyers have a floor to lean against. Below it, those buyers face pressure to exit, while sellers gain another level against which to define risk.

The former floor now becomes a ceiling to watch on a recovery.

Channel support gives buyers a foothold

Today’s low stalled near a lower channel trendline on the hourly chart. Buyers have leaned against that support, producing a modest bounce, with the price now trading above and below $3900.

Holding the trendline gives buyers an opportunity to slow the decline and attempt a corrective recovery. It also provides a close risk level: if support breaks, the reason for buying against it weakens.

A bounce alone, however, does not change the broader bearish picture. Buyers need to reclaim resistance to demonstrate that they can take back some control.

What next? Watch support below and the broken swing area above

If buyers can keep the price above the lower channel trendline, the next upside target is the $3942.71–$3959.37 swing area. Expect that zone to act as a test of the recovery. Sellers may lean against it, while a move back above would strengthen the buyers’ case and take some pressure off the downside.

Conversely, a break below the trendline and today’s low near $3891 would open the door to another extension lower.

Sellers retain control. Buyers have support to lean against, but they still have something to prove. The trendline defines the immediate downside risk, while the broken swing area defines the next upside hurdle.

Amazon: Strong growth comes with a heavy spending bill

For Amazon, the concern centers on spending and cash flow. AWS continues to grow strongly, but building the infrastructure to support that demand requires enormous capital investment. The AI trade faces a tougher test

Together, the reports challenge an important assumption behind the technology rally: that strong AI demand will be enough to support higher stock prices.

Demand can remain strong while the spending needed to meet it weighs on cash flow and profitability. When expectations are already elevated, investors have less patience for uncertainty about the timing and size of future returns.

item.title: Bitcoin sellers jump on the risk-off bandwagon
item.description:
With US and European stocks moving lower, bitcoin is following the risk-off sentiment. However, the move also has a technical catalyst: a break below the consolidation range that had contained the price since October 22.

That range extended from $79,146 on the downside to $81,930 on the topside. Over the last 24 hours, sellers pushed through the floor, triggering downside momentum that carried the price to $76,320.

The break gave sellers more control. The question now is whether they can extend that advantage through the next key support area.

Buyers find a reason to lean against support

The low stalled about $174 above the rising 100-day moving average at $76,146. Just below that moving average sits the 38.2% retracement of the advance from the late-June low at $76,052.

Together, those levels create a support zone between $76,052 and $76,146.

When two technical measures converge, they give traders a more clearly defined area to assess the next move. Dip buyers can lean against that support with limited risk, provided they are prepared to exit if the price breaks below and stays below it.

That does not guarantee a lasting bottom. It gives buyers a location where the potential reward can be weighed against a defined risk.

The initial rebound carried bitcoin to $78,559, but buyers could not sustain the recovery. The price has since rotated back toward $77,208, keeping the support zone in focus.

The old floor becomes the upside barometer

For buyers, holding support is only the first step. They also need to reclaim broken resistance.

The key level is $79,146, the former floor of the consolidation range. A break below support often turns that same level into resistance as sellers lean against it and trapped buyers use a rebound to exit.

As long as bitcoin stays below $79,146, sellers retain the advantage from the breakdown. A recovery above that level—and an ability to stay above it—would raise the possibility of a failed break lower.

That would start to worry sellers looking for further downside and put the upper boundary of the old range at $81,930 back on the radar.

Before then, the rebound high at $78,559 provides an interim upside hurdle.

Sellers need to break the support confluence

For sellers, the next task is clear: push below the 100-day moving average at $76,146 and the 38.2% retracement at $76,052, then keep the price below that area.

The 38.2% retracement is an important barometer when assessing a correction within a broader advance. Holding above it keeps the pullback relatively contained. Breaking below it would strengthen the case that a deeper correction is developing.

A brief move below support followed by a quick recovery would be less convincing. Sellers need sustained trading below the zone to confirm that the next downside break has traction.

Let the levels define the risk

War uncertainty, inflation concerns, worries about slower growth, and falling stock markets make the bearish case easy to understand. The break away from the 100- and 200-hour moving averages, followed by the move below consolidation support, adds technical weight to that story.

Nevertheless, a bearish narrative still needs a risk level.

For sellers, $79,146 is the key upside barometer. A sustained recovery above it would weaken the breakdown.

For dip buyers, $76,052–$76,146 is the key support zone. A sustained break below it would undermine the argument for buying against that confluence.

The battle lines are drawn. Sellers control the price below the old floor, while buyers have a defined support area where they can attempt to slow—or reverse—the decline.

  • Employment wages +0.7% vs +0.9% prior quarter

The US Employment Cost Index (ECI) increased by 0.8% q/q in the third quarter, with both wages and salaries and benefit costs contributing to the increase. Wages and salaries rose 0.7%, while benefit costs increased 0.9% compared with the previous quarter.

On an annual basis, total compensation costs for civilian workers increased by 3.4%, with wages and salaries rising 3.1% and benefit costs accelerating by 3.9%. The figures show that labour cost pressures remain relatively contained, although benefits continue to increase faster than wages.

Looking at private industry, compensation costs also increased by 0.8% q/q and 3.4% y/y. However, inflation-adjusted wages and salaries declined by 0.6% over the year, as nominal wage growth is still failing to keep pace with consumer price increases. The continued gap between nominal and inflation-adjusted wage growth also highlights the pressure households are facing from higher living costs.

For background, the Employment Cost Index (ECI) is a quarterly report from the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) that measures the change in the total cost of labor for businesses. The Fed considers the ECI the "gold standard" for measuring wage inflation because it is more precise and comprehensive, the only drawback is that it's not as timely as the Average Hourly Earnings data.

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

Canada’s economy stalled for a second consecutive month in August, according to Statistics Canada’s gross domestic product (GDP) by industry report. The softer detail came in the forward estimate: output is projected to have declined 0.1% in September, suggesting the economy lost momentum heading into the end of the third quarter. The industry-based figures point to 0.3% quarterly growth in Q3, subject to confirmation in the official quarterly release.

August’s flat headline masked considerable movement underneath. Retail trade rebounded 1.2%, more than reversing July’s contraction, while machinery production and a recovery in petroleum refining supported manufacturing. Those gains were offset by weaker wholesale trade, lower public-sector activity and another decline in oil and gas extraction. Auto production was particularly weak, with motor vehicles and parts manufacturing down 5.8% amid a prolonged summer plant shutdown.

Quick analysis: Two flat months followed by a projected decline suggest an economy struggling to build momentum. The retail rebound is encouraging, but growth was narrow, with fewer than half of industrial sectors expanding. Some weakness reflects maintenance outages, auto shutdowns and the winding down of Census activity, which limits how much can be attributed to softer underlying demand.

For the Bank of Canada, the growth figures could strengthen the case for easier policy if inflation allows. In isolation, weaker growth would normally weigh on Canadian yields and the Canadian dollar, creating an upward bias for USDCAD. The next checkpoint is November 30, when September GDP and the official Q3 income-and-expenditure estimates are released.

What this report measures: GDP by industry tracks inflation-adjusted production across Canada’s economy. Monthly changes show whether activity is expanding or contracting and which industries are driving it. The advance estimate is preliminary and subject to revision; the official quarterly income-and-expenditure report provides a separate measure of overall growth.

Amazon and Intel deepen the technology selloff

Amazon missed expectations for both earnings and revenue. Intel beat adjusted EPS estimates but missed revenue expectations, and its shares are suffering a much larger decline.

The broader question for investors remains: Are the earnings and future cash flows strong enough to justify the spending and valuations associated with AI?

The morning after the ECB left rates unchanged, officials are reinforcing the message that the inflation battle is unfinished. The common thread is a willingness to tighten further, with differences over how quickly action may be needed and how much tightening financial markets are already delivering.

Martin Kocher — a conditional warning about further tightening

Kocher said inflation risks have clearly increased and that a monetary policy response will be necessary if conditions do not improve soon. His comments suggest limited patience with persistent inflation pressure, while acknowledging the risks of acting prematurely.

The message for traders: yesterday’s unchanged decision should not be interpreted as confidence that inflation is under control.

Fabio Panetta — further hikes may be needed, but bond yields matter

Panetta said more rate increases may be necessary and warned that the increase in core inflation could become more pronounced early next year. However, he also stressed that the ECB must consider the recent rise in longer-term bond yields when calibrating policy.

Higher market borrowing costs can restrain demand without an additional ECB hike. Panetta also left room to adjust policy promptly if international conditions improve or financial tensions slow inflation.

His message is conditional: further tightening remains possible, but the ECB must assess how much restraint is already working through the economy.

Joachim Nagel — ready to act, with limited second-round effects so far

Nagel said policymakers would act decisively if needed, while noting that significant second-round effects have not appeared thus far.

That distinction matters. An energy-price shock can lift headline inflation directly. The greater concern is whether businesses and workers respond in ways that embed higher inflation in broader prices and wages.

The overall ECB message: The hold preserves flexibility, but further hikes remain an option. Persistent core inflation would strengthen the case for action, while higher bond yields and an improvement in the energy outlook could reduce the need for additional tightening.

Trump talks up an end to the Iran war, but oil moves higher (and the stocks are tumbling ahead of the election next week)

item.title: Eurozone Q3 GDP beats expectations but the growth surprise comes with a catch
item.description:
• Eurozone Q3 preliminary GDP +0.4% vs +0.2% q/q expected
  • Prior +0.6%
  • Eurozone Q3 preliminary GDP +1.3% vs +1.1% y/y expected
  • Prior +1.2%

Well, well, well. Would you look at that. The euro area economy has managed to pull a rabbit out of the hat, delivering a better-than-expected Q3 GDP reading at first glance. But before we start popping the champagne, there's a catch or two worth considering when you look at the details.

To start, quarterly growth did still slow down to 0.4% in the third quarter - down from 0.6% in the second quarter. So while the headline surprise is encouraging, the underlying momentum isn't quite as impressive as it might seem.

And when you drill deeper into the details, that is when things start to get a bit more interesting.

Of note, Ireland leads the pack with a whopping 5.5% quarterly expansion in Q3. Having said that, Ireland has a knack for notoriously volatile GDP figures in the past year and that always warrants some caution. The expansion here was primarily driven by strong activity in multinational-dominated industries, specifically information and communication and manufacturing.

For some context, Ireland's headline growth figure is often a distorted gauge of domestic economic health. That is because it is heavily influenced by contract manufacturing and global profits of multinational corporations that largely flow back to foreign shareholders rather than translating directly into local living standards.

Besides that, Spain continues to punch above its weight with 0.6% growth while the Netherlands also posted a respectable 0.6% increase.

Elsewhere though? The picture isn't so pretty.

Germany managed just 0.2% growth, Italy stagnated at 0.0%, and France even contracted by 0.1%. Now, that's hardly an endorsement of economic resilience across the biggest economies in the region.

So, what does this mean for the ECB?

We've seen inflation pressures heating up in France and Spain today even as the growth picture remains rather uneven. Meanwhile, German state inflation readings offered some relief but the broader concern remains that higher energy costs would eventually feed through to prices while weighing on economic activity.

And that is precisely the kind of stagflationary squeeze policymakers would want to avoid at this juncture.

So the real question now is whether the euro area can maintain its growth momentum as higher prices are going to squeeze households and businesses more and more in the months ahead. The latest report today might suggest that growth conditions are holding up a little bit better than feared, but whether that remains the case heading into Q4 will be a different story altogether.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: German state inflation cools in October, but will that ease the ECB's headache?
item.description:
The state readings released around the same time:

After the acceleration in September, headline inflation is seen cooling back a little in German states. While base effects are part of the reason, the re-implementation of specific energy tax reductions and fuel discounts enacted at the start of the month are arguably also playing a part here.

So, that is leading to cooler price pressures overall but still relatively elevated when compared to the months before this.

Putting the estimates together, it offers an indication that German inflation is set to decline at the national level as well. Headline annual inflation is expected to drop to 3.0% in October from 3.3% last month, with the state readings above pointing to a modest likelihood that we might even see a reading below the 3% mark.

In any case, just keep in mind though that the state readings aren't a perfect proxy for the national figure. There can still be some deviation when the preliminary numbers are released later. However, they have historically been a useful gauge and today's readings arguably point to some downside risk to the 3.0% consensus, with a national CPI reading around 2.9% now looking quite plausible.

For the ECB, the readings here will just complicate things further as the economic backdrop is reflecting flagging growth conditions amid the risk of price pressures accelerating further. While German inflation may not have jumped in October, there are signs elsewhere that inflation is starting to spread more broadly as seen with France and Spain earlier.

So, that will just keep the pressure on policymakers to act again in December while having to consider if doing too much could risk sending the euro area economy over the edge.
